cases.reason: The live divergence §4 exists to fix: keys z (U+007A), Ｚ (U+FF3A) and 😀 (U+1F600) sort as z, Ｚ, 😀 under ascending code-point order, but a binding sorting by UTF-16 code unit instead produces z, 😀, Ｚ, since 😀's surrogate pair begins at U+D800, below U+FF3A. Measured: reverting compareCodePoints to plain string comparison and re-running the corpus, this is caught by 0 of the other 21 cases — none of them puts an astral key beside one in U+E000-U+FFFF, so this is the corpus's sole witness to the bug.
Ordinary lexicographic ordering of plain ASCII keys, the baseline §4 case every ordering variant is measured against.
The empty string is the shortest possible key and, having no code points at all, MUST sort first under ascending code-point order.
Pins the exact upper boundary §5 names: ±(2⁵³−1). One past it is number-above-safe-range-rejected.
1e21 is what JS's own Number#toString would otherwise render in exponential form; §5 requires it be rejected instead of divergently serialized.
The lower boundary companion to number-max-safe-integer — §5's bound is symmetric (±(2⁵³−1)), and only testing the positive side would leave the negative half unpinned.
1.5's value has a nonzero fractional part, which §5 requires be rejected as non-integer-number rather than truncated or rounded.

JSON.parse("1.0") returns the JavaScript number 1 — the literal is destroyed before canonicalize ever runs. Python decodes the same text to a float and Go's UseNumber keeps json.Number("1.0"); all three MUST answer 1, holding §5 to the value rather than to whichever literal a binding's own decoder happened to see.

Each runtime reaches this differently — JSON.parse yields Infinity, json.loads yields inf, and Go's UseNumber yields a json.Number whose Float64() overflows — so this is the one case that forces all three to agree on the token. Measured: caught by 0 of the other 21 cases; a TypeScript implementation checking integrality before finiteness answers non-integer-number here while Python and Go answer number-out-of-range. That exact divergence was live in this shipment's first TypeScript implementation and was found by review, not by a test.

A negative zero already satisfies "the value's magnitude is a whole number", so §5's integral-value rule applies to it directly rather than as a separate exception; String(-0) would otherwise emit "0" only by JS coincidence, so this case pins the OUTPUT rather than relying on that coincidence.
§6 explicitly forbids escaping <, > and & — forbidding what encoding/json does by default in Go. A binding using Go's default HTML-escaping json.Marshal would fail this case.

Canonicalization is byte-preserving: a publisher whose editor emits NFD is signed in NFD. A binding that normalizes to NFC before encoding would collapse this to the single code point U+00E9 and fail the byte-equality assertion.
The anti-vacuity companion to string-nfd-preserved: byte-preservation cuts both ways, so a binding that decomposes to NFD before encoding would also fail this case.
§6 requires the short forms \b, \f, \n, \r and \t where they apply, rather than the generic \u00XX form every one of them could also be written in.
§6 requires lowercase \u00XX for every control code point in U+0000-U+001F that has no short escape — this pins both the form and the required lowercase hex digits.

§6 names exactly three things a conformant encoder must escape: the quote, the backslash, and the control range. This pins the first two together, since a binding that escapes only one of them still passes half the corpus.
Many JSON serializers escape the solidus as \/ by convention (it is legal, not required, JSON); §6 does not list it among the three required escapes, so a conformant encoder must leave it alone.

§6 requires every code point outside the escaped set be emitted literally, without exception — including one that needs a UTF-16 surrogate pair to represent in a 16-bit string type, which is exactly what distinguishes this from string-hex-control-escape.

§7's boundary is inclusive: a value at exactly depth 32 is within bounds. This is the accepting half of the boundary pair with depth-33-rejected — without it, an off-by-one binding that rejects at 32 instead of 33 would still pass the corpus.
The rejecting half of the boundary pair. §7 requires strictly greater than 32 to fail, so this is the first depth a conformant binding must refuse.
§8's whole purpose: the bytes that get signed must not include the signature that will cover them. A binding that forgets to strip signature would sign a payload no verifier could reproduce.

The anti-vacuity companion to manifest-strips-top-level-signature: stripping is shallow only. A binding that recursively strips every member named signature regardless of depth would silently drop data a publisher intended to sign, and this case is the one that would catch it.
